hern-n-cort-s.name: Hernán Cortés
hern-n-cort-s.summary: A Spanish conquistador and writer (c. 1485–1547) who defied Cuba's governor to press his expedition, allying with rival indigenous groups to overthrow the Aztec Empire; later made Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca.

tenochtitlan.name: Tenochtitlan
tenochtitlan.summary: The Aztec capital built on an island in Lake Texcoco, founded around 1325, that grew into the largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas before its capture in 1521.

q-eqchi.name: Qʼeqchiʼ
q-eqchi.summary: A Maya people of Guatemala, Belize and Mexico, originally centered in the Verapaz region before conquest-era displacement spread their communities more widely than any other Maya group.

casta.name: Casta paintings
casta.summary: A Spanish and Portuguese term meaning 'lineage,' historically used as a racial and social label in colonial Spanish America; 18th-century casta paintings depicted an invented hierarchy of mixed-race families.

new-spain.name: New Spain
new-spain.summary: A Spanish colonial territory founded after the 1521 conquest of the Aztec Empire, with its capital at Mexico City, covering much of Mexico, Central America and parts of the Caribbean; made a viceroyalty in 1535.

mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral.name: Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral
mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral.summary: The cathedral church of the Catholic Archdiocese of Mexico, built in stages from 1573 to 1813 atop the former Aztec sacred precinct in Mexico City's historic center, blending Gothic, Baroque and Neoclassical styles.

tepotzotl-n.name: Tepotzotlán
tepotzotl-n.summary: A town near Mexico City that became a major colonial educational center after Jesuits founded the College of San Francisco Javier there in 1580; its complex is now a museum of viceregal art.

fernando-de-alva-cort-s-ixtlilx-chitl.name: Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxóchitl
fernando-de-alva-cort-s-ixtlilx-chitl.summary: A nobleman of partial Aztec descent in colonial New Spain, born between 1568 and 1580 and died in 1648, best known for chronicling indigenous Aztec history.

tetzcoco-altepetl.name: Tetzcoco
tetzcoco-altepetl.summary: A major Acolhua city-state on Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico, one of the three members of the Aztec Triple Alliance and, after Tenochtitlan, among the largest cities in central Mexico before the Spanish conquest.

churrigueresque.name: Churrigueresque
churrigueresque.summary: A Spanish Baroque style of elaborate sculptural ornament that emerged in Spain in the late 17th century and was used until about 1750, marked by extreme, florid decorative detailing on building façades.

crist-bal-de-villalpando.name: Cristóbal de Villalpando
crist-bal-de-villalpando.summary: A Baroque painter (c. 1649–1714) from New Spain who produced many large works now in Mexican cathedrals, including Mexico City and Puebla.

juan-gerson.name: Juan Gerson
juan-gerson.summary: An indigenous Nahua painter active around 1562, working in Tecamachalco, Puebla; long mistakenly thought to be a European-trained Flemish artist until his indigenous identity was rediscovered in 1962.

florentine-codex.name: Florentine Codex
florentine-codex.summary: A 16th-century ethnographic study of Aztec culture, religion and history, compiled from 1545 to 1590 by friar Bernardino de Sahagún with Nahua collaborators, in bilingual Nahuatl-Spanish text with over 2,000 illustrations.

bernardino-de-sahag-n.name: Bernardino de Sahagún
bernardino-de-sahag-n.summary: A Franciscan friar (c.1499–1590) who spent over 50 years studying Aztec culture and language in colonial Mexico, compiling the bilingual Florentine Codex.

mexica.name: Mexica
mexica.summary: A Nahuatl-speaking people of the Valley of Mexico who ruled the Triple Alliance, commonly called the Aztec Empire, and founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 before Spanish conquest ended their rule in 1521.

nahuatl.name: Nahuatl
nahuatl.summary: A language of the Uto-Aztecan family spoken in central Mexico since at least the 7th century CE, once the prestige language of the Aztec Empire.

xicochi.name: Xicochi
xicochi.summary: A 17th-century motet by Gaspar Fernandes, organist of Puebla Cathedral, showing the influence of indigenous Nahua culture on colonial Spanish music.

gaspar-fernandes.name: Gaspar Fernandes
gaspar-fernandes.summary: Portuguese-Mexican composer and organist (1566–1629) active in the cathedrals of Santiago de Guatemala and Puebla de los Ángeles in New Spain.

puebla-cathedral.name: Puebla Cathedral
puebla-cathedral.summary: The cathedral of Puebla, Mexico, consecrated in 1649 as the first grand cathedral built in the Americas; construction took 74 years under three successive Spanish kings.

nahuas.name: Nahuas
nahuas.summary: An Indigenous people of Mexico, the largest such group there, including the Aztec (Mexica) and their historic rivals the Tlaxcallans, who speak Nahuatl.

peter-paul-rubens.name: Peter Paul Rubens
peter-paul-rubens.summary: Flemish Baroque painter and diplomat (1577–1640), considered the most influential artist of the Flemish Baroque, known for dramatic, sensuous religious and mythological works.

juan-correa.name: Juan Correa
juan-correa.summary: Mexican painter (1646–1716), most active from 1671 to 1716, distinguished among late 17th- and early 18th-century artists in colonial Mexico.

jos-de-ibarra.name: José de Ibarra
jos-de-ibarra.summary: New Spanish painter (1688–1756) trained under Juan Correa, and one of the leading figures in early 18th-century painting in colonial Mexico, blending Italian and French influences.

miguel-cabrera-painter.name: Miguel Cabrera
miguel-cabrera-painter.summary: A Mexican painter of the late Baroque (1695–1768), recognized as New Spain's greatest painter, known for religious art and finely regarded casta paintings.

luis-de-mena.name: Luis de Mena
luis-de-mena.summary: An 18th-century Mexican painter best known for a 1750 casta painting, now in Madrid, uniquely combining Mexico's colonial caste system with the Virgin of Guadalupe.

our-lady-of-guadalupe.name: Virgin of Guadalupe
our-lady-of-guadalupe.summary: A Catholic title of the Virgin Mary linked to reported 1531 apparitions to Juan Diego in Mexico; her venerated image is enshrined in a Mexico City basilica, one of the world's most-visited shrines.

spanish-conquest-of-yucat-n.name: Spanish conquest of Yucatán
spanish-conquest-of-yucat-n.summary: The Spanish campaign against the Late Postclassic Maya states of the Yucatán Peninsula, hindered by the region's political fragmentation and prolonged by Maya guerrilla resistance.

nojpet-n.name: Nojpetén
nojpet-n.summary: Capital of the Itza Maya kingdom of Petén Itzá, on an island in Lake Petén Itzá in Guatemala; it was the last independent Maya kingdom, falling to the Spanish in 1697.

lake-pet-n-itz.name: Lake Petén Itzá
lake-pet-n-itz.summary: The third-largest lake in Guatemala, in the northern Petén Department; it has no surface outflow, and its archaeological richness draws about 150,000 tourists a year.

itza-people.name: Itza
itza-people.summary: A Maya ethnic group descended from the Chontal Chanes who settled around Lake Petén Itzá and remained independent there until conquered by the Spanish in 1697.

kowoj.name: Kowoj
kowoj.summary: Maya group and polity of the Late Postclassic period (about 1250–1697) that claimed descent from migrants out of Mayapan after its collapse in 1441, identified by a distinctive style of temple architecture.

zacpeten.name: Zacpeten
zacpeten.summary: A pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site in northern Guatemala, notable as home to one of the few Maya communities that kept its independence into early Spanish colonial times.

francisco-hern-ndez-de-c-rdoba-yucat-n-c.name: Francisco Hernández de Córdoba
francisco-hern-ndez-de-c-rdoba-yucat-n-c.summary: Spanish conquistador (c. 1467–1517) who led the 1517 expedition that produced the first European accounts of the Yucatán Peninsula, dying from wounds suffered fighting the Maya.

conspiracy-of-the-machetes.name: Conspiracy of the Machetes
conspiracy-of-the-machetes.summary: An unsuccessful 1799 rebellion against Spanish rule in New Spain, now seen in Mexico as an early precursor to the Mexican War of Independence.

classic-maya-language.name: Classic Maya
classic-maya-language.summary: The oldest attested Mayan language, the main language of pre-Columbian Maya inscriptions and ancestor of the modern Cholan languages.

popol-vuh.name: Popol Vuh
popol-vuh.summary: Foundational sacred narrative of the Kʼicheʼ Maya people of Guatemala, containing their creation myth and history; preserved orally until it was written down around 1550.

rabinal-ach.name: Rabinal Achí
rabinal-ach.summary: A Maya theatrical dance-drama in the Kʼicheʼ language, still performed annually in Rabinal, Guatemala, and one of the few surviving pre-colonial performance pieces, centered on a historic feud between two cities.

cantares-mexicanos.name: Cantares Mexicanos
cantares-mexicanos.summary: A 16th-century manuscript collection of 91 Nahuatl songs or poems, the largest surviving collection of traditional Nahuatl song, now held in Mexico City's National Library.

chilam-balam.name: Chilam Balam
chilam-balam.summary: A collection of handwritten Yucatec Maya manuscripts from the 17th and 18th centuries, blending Indigenous and Spanish traditions on history, prophecy, and astronomy.

yucatec-maya-language.name: Yucatec Maya
yucatec-maya-language.summary: A Mayan language spoken in the Yucatán Peninsula and part of northern Belize, called maayaʼ tʼaan by its own speakers.

andr-s-de-olmos.name: Andrés de Olmos
andr-s-de-olmos.summary: Spanish Franciscan priest and grammarian (c. 1485-1571) who wrote the first grammar in the New World, of the Classical Nahuatl language.

horacio-carochi.name: Horacio Carochi
horacio-carochi.summary: Jesuit priest and grammarian (1586 to 1666), born in Florence and died in New Spain, known for his grammar of Classical Nahuatl.

romances-de-los-se-ores-de-nueva-espa-a.name: Romances de los señores de Nueva España
romances-de-los-se-ores-de-nueva-espa-a.summary: A 16th-century compilation of Nahuatl songs, several attributed to ruler Nezahualcoyotl, preserved with a 1582 Spanish-language account by Juan Bautista Pomar.
romances-de-los-se-ores-de-nueva-espa-a.source_title: Romances de los señores de Nueva España

colegio-de-santa-cruz-de-tlatelolco.name: Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco
colegio-de-santa-cruz-de-tlatelolco.summary: The first European school of higher learning in the Americas, founded by Franciscans in 1536 in Mexico City to prepare Native American boys for the Catholic priesthood.
colegio-de-santa-cruz-de-tlatelolco.source_title: Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco

diego-de-landa.name: Diego de Landa
diego-de-landa.summary: Spanish Franciscan bishop, 1524 to 1579, who burned Maya manuscripts while campaigning against idolatry, yet whose own writings on Maya culture became a key source for understanding Maya civilization.

relaci-n-de-las-cosas-de-yucat-n.name: Relación de las cosas de Yucatán
relaci-n-de-las-cosas-de-yucat-n.summary: A 1566 book by Diego de Landa cataloguing Maya words and hieroglyphs; its "de Landa alphabet" proved vital to later decipherment of Maya writing.
relaci-n-de-las-cosas-de-yucat-n.source_title: Relación de las cosas de Yucatán

francisco-xim-nez.name: Francisco Ximénez
francisco-xim-nez.summary: Dominican priest (1666–c. 1729) who transcribed and translated the Popol Vuh, an indigenous Maya narrative, while serving as a parish priest in Guatemala in the early 1700s.

codex-mendoza.name: Codex Mendoza
codex-mendoza.summary: An Aztec codex from around 1541 recording Aztec rulers, conquests, and daily life, commissioned by New Spain's viceroy Antonio de Mendoza.

diego-dur-n.name: Diego Durán
diego-dur-n.summary: Dominican friar, c. 1537 to 1588, author of one of the earliest Western accounts of Aztec history and culture, fluent in Nahuatl and able to draw on native informants and codices.

moctezuma-ii.name: Moctezuma II
moctezuma-ii.summary: Ninth emperor of the Aztec Empire, reigning from 1502 or 1503 until his death in 1520 during the Spanish conquest of Tenochtitlan led by Hernán Cortés. Under him the empire reached its greatest territorial extent.

quetzalc-tl.name: Quetzalcoatl
quetzalc-tl.summary: A major Aztec deity, the 'Feathered Serpent', linked to wind, the planet Venus, the sun, learning and the priesthood; later accounts conflated him with a legendary Toltec ruler.

charles-v-holy-roman-emperor.name: Charles V
charles-v-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain (1500–1558) whose Habsburg realms in Europe and the Americas were together called 'the empire on which the sun never sets'.

juan-bautista-pomar.name: Juan Bautista Pomar
juan-bautista-pomar.summary: Mestizo historian and writer (c. 1535–after 1601), great-grandson of Texcoco ruler Nezahualcoyotl, whose Relación de Texcoco and compiled Nahuatl poetry are major sources on prehispanic Aztec history.

philip-ii-of-spain.name: Philip II of Spain
philip-ii-of-spain.summary: King of Spain from 1556 and Portugal from 1580, under whom Spain reached its height of power, including the conquest of the Philippines, named in his honor.

bernal-d-az-del-castillo.name: Bernal Díaz del Castillo
bernal-d-az-del-castillo.summary: A Spanish conquistador (c.1492–1584) who fought in the conquest of the Aztec Empire under Hernán Cortés and later wrote a firsthand account of the conquest.

toribio-de-benavente.name: Motolinía
toribio-de-benavente.summary: Franciscan missionary, one of the Twelve Apostles of Mexico who arrived in New Spain in 1524, whose writings are a key source on Nahua history and evangelization.

zacatecas.name: Zacatecas
zacatecas.summary: A state in north-central Mexico, known for rich silver deposits, colonial architecture, and its role in the Mexican Revolution.

chichimeca.name: Chichimeca
chichimeca.summary: A term the Aztecs and Spanish used for nomadic and semi-nomadic peoples of north-central Mexico, comparable to "barbarian," who fiercely resisted Spanish expansion.

chichimeca-war.name: Chichimeca War
chichimeca-war.summary: A 1550–1600 conflict between Spain and Chichimeca peoples over silver-rich territory in north-central Mexico, the longest and costliest war between Spaniards and Indigenous peoples in the Americas.

mart-n-de-urs-a.name: Martín de Ursúa
mart-n-de-urs-a.summary: Spanish conquistador and colonial governor (1653–1715) who in 1696–97 led the force that captured Nojpetén, the last independent Maya stronghold, and later governed Yucatán and the Philippines.

tlacopan.name: Tlacopan
tlacopan.summary: A Tepanec/Mexica city-state on the western shore of Lake Texcoco, one of the three cities in the Aztec Triple Alliance that ruled central Mexico from 1428.

lvaro-manrique-de-z-iga-1st-marquess-of-.name: Álvaro Manrique de Zúñiga
lvaro-manrique-de-z-iga-1st-marquess-of-.summary: Spanish nobleman who served as the seventh viceroy of New Spain, governing from 1585 to 1590.
lvaro-manrique-de-z-iga-1st-marquess-of-.source_title: Álvaro Manrique de Zúñiga, 1st Marquess of Villamanrique

council-of-the-indies.name: Council of the Indies
council-of-the-indies.summary: The chief administrative and advisory body for Spain's American territories, established in 1524 by Charles V and based in Madrid from 1561 until its abolition in 1834.

captaincy-general-of-guatemala.name: Captaincy General of Guatemala
captaincy-general-of-guatemala.summary: A Spanish colonial administrative division under the viceroyalty of New Spain, covering present-day Guatemala, Chiapas, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica.

antigua-guatemala.name: Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala
antigua-guatemala.summary: The historical name of Antigua Guatemala, a city that served as capital of the Captaincy General of Guatemala from 1543 to 1773, known for its Spanish Baroque architecture.

pedro-de-alvarado.name: Pedro de Alvarado
pedro-de-alvarado.summary: Spanish conquistador (c. 1485–1541) who helped conquer the Aztec Empire and led the conquest of much of Central America, though notorious for cruelty and greed.

pet-n-basin.name: Petén
pet-n-basin.summary: A subregion of the Maya Lowlands in northern Guatemala where major Maya centers such as Tikal and Calakmul flourished.

diego-carrillo-de-mendoza-1st-marquess-o.name: Diego Carrillo de Mendoza
diego-carrillo-de-mendoza-1st-marquess-o.summary: Spanish cavalry general who served as viceroy of Aragon, then as viceroy of New Spain from 1621 to 1624, dying in 1631.
diego-carrillo-de-mendoza-1st-marquess-o.source_title: Diego Carrillo de Mendoza, 1st Marquess of Gelves

yalain.name: Yalain
yalain.summary: A proposed Maya polity of the Postclassic period (c. 1000–1697) based near the central Petén lakes of northern Guatemala.

kejache.name: Kejache
kejache.summary: A Maya people of northern Guatemala's Petén Basin at the time of Spanish contact in the 17th century, first reached by Hernán Cortés in 1525.

tlahuicole.name: Tlahuicole
tlahuicole.summary: A Tlaxcaltec warrior, about 1497 to 1518, noted for his skill in battle and his ethical conduct.

tlaxcala-nahua-state.name: Tlaxcala
tlaxcala-nahua-state.summary: A pre-Columbian city-state in central Mexico that resisted Aztec domination for generations and later allied with the Spanish during their conquest of the Aztec Empire.

pur-pecha-empire.name: Purépecha Empire
pur-pecha-empire.summary: A pre-Columbian state covering roughly today's Michoacán, Mexico, and nearby areas, the second-largest in Mesoamerica by the Spanish conquest; founded in the early 14th century and conquered by Spain in 1530.

juana-in-s-de-la-cruz.name: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
juana-in-s-de-la-cruz.summary: A Hieronymite nun, writer, philosopher and poet of the Baroque period (1648–1695), nicknamed 'the Tenth Muse'; considered one of the most important female writers in Spanish-language literature.

mexican-inquisition.name: Mexican Inquisition
mexican-inquisition.summary: An extension of the Spanish Inquisition into New Spain, officially active from 1571 to 1820, prosecuting non-Catholics and unorthodox believers, with an estimated 50 people executed.

altepetl.name: Altepetl
altepetl.summary: Local, ethnically based city-state political unit of pre-Columbian Nahuatl-speaking societies, each with its own ruler, origin story, and sense of identity.

archdiocese-of-mexico.name: Archdiocese of Mexico
archdiocese-of-mexico.summary: The Catholic Church's ecclesiastical territory in Mexico City, made a diocese in 1530 and raised to an archdiocese in 1546.

k-iche-language.name: Kʼicheʼ language
k-iche-language.summary: A Mayan language spoken by over a million people in Guatemala's central highlands, the country's second most common language, famous as the tongue of the Popol Vuh.

converso.name: Conversos
converso.summary: Jews, or their descendants, who converted to Catholicism in Spain or Portugal, especially in the 14th and 15th centuries, often under pressure from the Inquisition and expulsion decrees.
